worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-\frac{1}{2}x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/1d2a232b4351c84871d89ba25384aa53777760355ceea6458b07fba9c0a9ed78.png)

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=0
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line.

Since ${e}^{3t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/122759a459c8dd56dbe69c44c0da4ccffbbc660465fbedc7457e17b42430436e.png)

For this particular system, we have

$$
0<{\lambda }_{2}<{\lambda }_{1}
$$

thus, ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ is the dominant eigenvalue.

Since the dominant eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$  solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector  ${v}_{1}$ as they move away from the origin.

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/fcaa3ba63a1e6ad061eecf1f72caf3c9f8ba78b014eff044ee5be682e1325128.png)
